relationships.reason: Reversing a singly linked list in-place requires understanding the underlying Node class and basic pointer mechanics introduced in the singly linked list traversal.
Floyd's Tortoise and Hare cycle detection runs on a singly linked list, which fundamentally requires understanding the Node class structure and reference traversing defined in Chunk 8.
Merging two sorted linked lists manipulates Node links and constructs a new list structure, making standard singly linked list representation a strict prerequisite.
The balanced parentheses checker is a classic application of a Stack; students must understand basic LIFO stack operations (push, pop, peek) before applying them here.
Evaluating postfix expressions relies heavily on push and pop operations of a Stack to handle operators and operands.
A Min Stack is an advanced wrapper around a standard Stack that manages min tracking. Understanding the basic Stack structure is required first.
The naive recursive Fibonacci sequence is built on multi-branch recursion, which requires a prior understanding of simple linear recursion as demonstrated in the Factorial code.
Recursive binary search divides the search space using the same logical boundaries as iterative binary search; understanding the iterative version first is crucial.
Implementing binary search recursively requires a baseline understanding of recursive calls and base cases.
Finding the first and last occurrence modifies the standard iterative binary search algorithm to look for bounds. Standard binary search is a direct prerequisite.
Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that relies recursively on splitting lists and merging them back, requiring a baseline grasp of recursion.
Quick Sort relies on recursive partitioning of arrays, making basic recursive function flow a prerequisite.
Tree traversals require manipulating TreeNode objects (left, right, and value) which are defined in the BST insert and search module.
Level-order traversal operates on TreeNode instances, which are introduced and structured in Chunk 38.
Breadth-first level-order tree traversal requires using a queue (deque) to track nodes across levels in FIFO order.
Computing tree height requires traversing the tree nodes (TreeNode) defined in the basic tree chunk.
The height of a binary tree is calculated using a post-order recursive process, requiring foundational knowledge of recursion.
Validating a Binary Search Tree relies directly on checking the BST invariant (left < root < right) introduced in the BST insert/search chunk.
Finding the Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) in a BST leverages BST node ordering properties, which are defined and explored in Chunk 38.
The Kth largest element algorithm relies directly on the operations and properties of a min-heap (via heapq) introduced in Chunk 44.
Merging k sorted lists utilizes a min-heap structure to efficiently fetch the next smallest element, requiring the heapq API and heap concepts from Chunk 44.
Breadth-First Search traverses a graph represented as an adjacency list, which is introduced in Chunk 47.
BFS relies on a FIFO queue to explore nodes level-by-level, making the queue data structure a prerequisite.
Recursive DFS operates directly on the graph adjacency list structure introduced in Chunk 47.
DFS is implemented via recursive calls to backtrack along path branches, which requires basic recursive programming skills.
Cycle detection in directed graphs is an advanced DFS application that tracks back-edges using a recursion stack, requiring understanding of DFS traversal first.
Topological sorting processes graph vertices and edges, which relies on the adjacency list representation defined in Chunk 47.
Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm traverses graphs represented via adjacency lists with weighted edges.
Dijkstra's algorithm relies on a min-priority queue (min-heap) to select the next closest vertex with minimum distance.
Counting connected components requires looping through all nodes and running a complete recursive DFS for each unvisited component.
Memoized Fibonacci is introduced to address the exponential runtime and redundant subproblems of naive recursive Fibonacci, making Chunk 20 a prerequisite.
Permutation generation uses backtracking, which is a state-restoring form of recursion. Basic recursion is a mandatory prerequisite.
N-Queens is a complex constraint-satisfaction backtracking puzzle that requires understanding basic backtracking search state logic first.
Generating power sets utilizes standard state backtracking (choosing, recursing, and popping/undoing), which is introduced step-by-step in standard backtracking examples like permutations.
Kruskal's MST algorithm relies directly on the Union-Find data structure to prevent cycles when adding edges to the forest.
